title: Host Logs with journald
intro: Before any fancy log aggregation, there's the host's own journal. These filters get you from 'millions of lines' to 'the three lines that matter' in seconds.

steps.prompt: Show only error-level (and worse) messages from all services.
steps.fake_output:
Sep 27 09:12:44 db01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 920 (postgres)
Sep 27 09:40:02 db01 backup.sh[3100]: ERROR: disk write failed
steps.explanation: -p filters by syslog priority: err (3) and more severe (crit, alert, emerg).
steps.why: Filtering by priority across ALL services often reveals cross-service causes (like a kernel OOM) that looking at one service's logs never would.

steps.fake_output:
Sep 27 00:00:03 db01 systemd[1]: Starting Daily apt upgrade...
...
steps.explanation: --since accepts 'today', 'yesterday', '1 hour ago', or exact timestamps.
steps.why: Combine it: 'journalctl -u postgres --since "2026-09-27 09:00" --until "09:20"' zooms straight into an incident window.

steps.fake_output: Sep 27 09:12:44 db01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 920 (postgres)
steps.explanation: Equivalent to dmesg, but with real timestamps and persistent across reboots (if the journal is persistent).
steps.why: dmesg's ring buffer is lost on reboot; the journal keeps kernel messages from previous boots — add '-b -1' to see the previous boot, essential after a crash-and-reboot.

steps.prompt: Check how much disk space the journal is using.
steps.fake_output: Archived and active journals take up 11.8G in the file system.
steps.why: Unbounded journals are a real cause of full disks (see monitoring-incident-006). Limits belong in /etc/systemd/journald.conf (SystemMaxUse=).

steps.prompt: Delete archived journal entries older than 7 days.
steps.fake_output:
Deleted archived journal /var/log/journal/.../system@0005f2.journal (128.0M).
...
Vacuuming done, freed 10.2G of archived journals.
steps.explanation: Old archives are removed; the active journal is untouched.
steps.why: --vacuum-size=1G is the alternative when you care about disk rather than age. Either is a one-off fix; journald.conf limits make it permanent.
